extraction.coverage: Full text read: lines 0 to 5066 of the text file (EOF reached), covering abstract, introduction, Study 1 to Study 4 (method and results), discussion, limitations, use cases, conclusion, references, general appendix, Study 1 literature overview, Study 2 and Study 3 appendices. No Paul markup files were listed for this item ("(none)"), so paul_markup is empty. Nothing in the text concerns lobbying, legislative networks, path-finding, allocation, or text-as-data pipelines beyond literature mentions and one use-case paragraph; the only text-measurement point is the Aaldering and Vliegenthart (2016) computer-assisted content analysis reference.
extraction.research_question: How can political personality be assessed with a comprehensive, facet-level, contextualized, psychometrically validated inventory that works for (a) voters' ideal traits for politicians, (b) citizens' perceptions of actual politicians' traits, and (c) perceived self-other similarity between voters and politicians? (p.2, p.11-12)
extraction.theory: Bottom-up construction of 15 politically relevant personality facets, each located a posteriori in the nomological net of established models: NEO PI-R, BFI-2, IPIP-NEO (Big Five facets), HEXACO, Values-in-Action character strengths, the Agency/Communion "Big Two" (Abele et al., 2020), and the six-category political leadership trait scheme of Aaldering and Vliegenthart (2016) (Table 1, pp.14-16). Argues global frameworks (Big Five, Big Two) lack specificity and contextualization, while ad hoc political measures lack generalizability and create jingle/jangle problems (pp.4-6). Argues contextualized items referring to the political role outperform non-contextualized ones (Danner and Lechner, 2024; Shaffer and Postlethwaite, 2012) and that items should target observable behavioral cues because voters judge the public persona (pp.8-10). Flags ideological content in items (Hatemi and Verhulst, 2015) and social desirability bias (Backstrom et al., 2009) as threats to neutrality (pp.9-10).
extraction.data: Four German-language survey studies, unit = individual respondent rating self, an ideal politician, or a named real politician. Study 1 (pp.11-14, Table 1): no data sample; literature mapping and item pool construction (110-item pool). Study 2 (self-ratings, general population, pp.22-26): N = 404 after excluding 21 straight-liners (fieldwork Oct 2020; Respondi AG online panel, CAWI; German native speakers; quotas on age, gender, education from German census; 51.0% female; age M = 42.6, SD = 14.0, range 18-68; education 34.9% low, 33.2% intermediate, 31.9% high). Study 3 (other-ratings of ideal politician, pp.27-28): N = 589 after excluding 40 straight-liners (fieldwork May 2020; same sampling as Study 2; randomized male-politician (N = 289) vs female-politician (N = 300) prompts; 51.3% female; age M = 43.4, SD = 14.6, range 18-69). Study 4 (observer ratings of real politicians, pp.29-34): N = 211 after excluding 2 straight-liners (clickworker.de crowdsourcing, fieldwork April 2021; EUR 2.25 compensation; Trump n = 104, Merkel n = 107; 38.9% female; age M = 39.9, SD = 13.3, range 18-69; education 4.7% low, 19.0% intermediate, 76.3% high; authors describe sample as male-leaning, highly educated, and somewhat left-leaning). Study 2 used 110-item pool, planned missingness (three partial blocks A/B/C plus common block X, each respondent 85 of 110 items); Study 4 used 86 personality items plus catch-all candidate measures.
extraction.method: Item construction from explicit facet definitions with two disambiguating trait words per item and balanced positive/negative keying (pp.21-22). 5-point agreement scale (Study 2, 3) and 1-5 scale for facet composites (Study 4). Composite facet scores are prorated means of 4-item scales (Dedication & Sacrifice uses 2 items). Factorial validity: principal components analysis of ipsatized items (centered on each respondent's mean to remove acquiescence) with Horn (1965) parallel analysis, 1,000 random draws, run in Stata fapara (pp.24-25, 28, 30). Reliability: Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability omega from a CFA congeneric model (Raykov, 1997), Stata sem/relicoef (pp.25, 28, 30). Convergent validity: correlations of facet composites with BFI-2-XS domain scores and a three-item Machiavellianism scale (Study 2, Table 3); Study 4 correlations with catch-all candidate measures on 11-point scales (likeability feeling thermometer, vote propensity, honesty, competence, charisma, assertiveness, left-right placement and absolute ideological proximity). Group comparisons: Cohen's d for male vs female prompt (Study 3) and Trump vs Merkel means (Study 4), plus sociodemographic means (Table A3). PCA reported with orthogonal varimax rotation for the prototype and candidate composites (Figures A4, A7).
extraction.identification: None stated. The paper is psychometric and descriptive: cross-sectional survey correlations, mean differences, and factor structure. It does not claim causal identification. The text calls the Study 4 correlations "predictive validity" (p.36), but the analyses are concurrent associations among same-occasion ratings (Table 5).
extraction.scope: Population: German native-speaking adults in general population panels (Studies 2-3) and German native-speaking crowdsourced raters (Study 4). Institutional focus: individual politicians as perceived by voters; item wording references the political role. Targets in Study 4: Donald Trump (US former president) and Angela Merkel (German former chancellor). Era: fieldwork 2020-2021; the paper's literature runs to 2024. Language: German items with English translations in Table A2. The authors note that generalization to lesser-known politicians and to other countries is untested (p.38).

key_findings.finding: The framework has 15 politically relevant personality facets (e.g., Trust & Faith in Others; Compromise & Cooperativeness; Assertiveness & Will to take control; Dedication & Sacrifice), each mapped to HEXACO, Big Five, VIA, Agency/Communion, and the Aaldering and Vliegenthart (2016) traits.
key_findings.numbers: 15 facets; 4-item scales plus one 2-item scale (Dedication & Sacrifice)

key_findings.finding: Self-rated facet reliabilities (Study 2) were moderate to high for most facets but low for several.
key_findings.numbers: alpha .44-.87; omega .43-.84. Lowest: Loyalty to Principles alpha .44 / omega .46; Humility alpha .46 / omega .43; Compromise alpha .51 / omega .45. Highest: Dedication alpha .87 / omega .84 (2-item scale)

key_findings.finding: Self-rated facets converge with the expected Big Five domains in the BFI-2-XS (Study 2): trust, compromise and empathy track Agreeableness; passion tracks Extraversion; optimism and composure track Emotional Stability.
key_findings.numbers: Trust-A r = .50; Empathy-A r = .48; Compromise-A r = .33; Passion-E r = .57; Optimism-ES r = .63; Self-Confidence-ES r = .56; Manners-C r = .59; Creativity-O r = .33. Machiavellianism: Integrity r = -.44, Empathy r = -.44, Humility r = -.37

key_findings.finding: Intellect & Mental Acuity correlated unexpectedly with BFI-2 Emotional Stability, mostly driven by one depression item.
Essential unidimensionality for most facets in self-ratings, with Creativity & Problem-Solving the clear exception and Loyalty to Principles borderline.
key_findings.numbers: Horn parallel analysis retained one component for all facets except Creativity; 15 scales judged essentially unidimensional

key_findings.finding: Ideal-politician prototypes showed almost no dependence on the politician's gender. Only Assertiveness differed, and it was rated more desirable for a female politician.
key_findings.location: Study 3 results, p.28; Table A5, p.74
key_findings.numbers: |d| = .00-.19; Assertiveness d = .19, p = .025 (male N = 289, female N = 300)

key_findings.finding: Ideal-trait scale reliabilities were modest. Assertiveness yielded two factors because one item (power-hungry, claims leadership) loaded reversed.
key_findings.numbers: Text: alpha .40-.78, omega .55-.79. Table A4 gives alpha .53-.78 with Assertiveness not computed (n.c.)

key_findings.finding: Observer ratings of Trump and Merkel differed significantly on 14 of 15 facets. The clearest contrasts were Self-Confidence & Composure, Trust & Faith in Others, and Humility, with Trump lower; Trump was rated higher on Assertiveness, Passion, and Creativity. Loyalty to Principles showed no difference.
key_findings.numbers: Self-Confidence d = -3.31 (Trump M 1.80 vs Merkel M 4.20); Trust d = -2.15 (1.72 vs 3.23); Humility d = -3.27 (1.31 vs 3.69); Assertiveness d = 1.41 (4.12 vs 3.33); Passion d = .93 (3.55 vs 2.73); Creativity d = .45 (2.98 vs 2.63); Loyalty d = .00 (3.31 vs 3.31); Trump N = 104, Merkel N = 107

key_findings.finding: Facets correlate with catch-all candidate measures in theoretically expected ways. Compassion tracks likeability; Integrity and Honesty tracks honesty; general assertiveness tracks the Assertiveness facet.
key_findings.numbers: Empathy-likeability r = .70 (Trump) / .76 (Merkel); Integrity-honesty r = .70 / .80; Assertiveness-general assertiveness r = .42 / .53; Passion-charisma r = .58 / .61 (Trump / Merkel); Intellect-vote propensity r = .67 (Trump); Creativity-vote propensity r = .71 (Merkel)

key_findings.finding: Ideological proximity to the target correlates with several facet ratings, consistent with political opponents attributing more undesirable traits. The authors interpret this as bias in observer ratings.
key_findings.location: Table 5 column Prx, pp.33-34; text pp.32-33
key_findings.numbers: Intellect-proximity r = .48 (Trump); Integrity-proximity r = .46 (Trump) and .36 (Merkel); Creativity-proximity r = .37 (Merkel)

key_findings.finding: Observer ratings of Trump and Merkel were reported to show a reliability range that does not match Table A7 for two facets.
key_findings.numbers: Text: alpha .40-.93, omega .48-.94. Table A7 lists Loyalty to Principles alpha .34 (omega n.c.) and Assertiveness alpha .40 / omega .48. Loyalty may be bidimensional in observer ratings (footnote 5, p.30)

key_findings.finding: Study 2 Discussion states the Study 1 item pool was reduced to four core items per facet (60 total). The Study 2 section describes 58 retained items (14 four-item scales plus one two-item scale).
key_findings.numbers: 58 vs 60 items; 110-item initial pool

measures: 15 PoliPers facets, self-report and observer versions, with 4-item scales (Dedication & Sacrifice: 2 items); 5-point agreement scale (Studies 2-3), 1-5 composites (Study 4)
Opposite poles defined per facet, e.g., Reserve & Reluctance to Trust; Rigidity & Inflexibility; Apathy & Indifference (pp.17-21)
BFI-2-XS (Rammstedt et al., 2018) domain scores for convergence (Study 2)
Three-item Machiavellianism scale (Moshagen et al., 2020) for convergence (Study 2)

Catch-all candidate measures in Study 4, 11-point scales from AUTNES 2013 and GLES-style items: left-right placement (with absolute ideological proximity), likeability (feeling thermometer), propensity to vote, honesty, competence, charisma, assertiveness (Table A8 wordings, pp.74-76)
Ipsatized composite scores; Cronbach alpha and composite omega (Raykov, 1997)
limitations: Social desirability and ideological bias may affect both self-reports and observer ratings (p.37, citing Rothschild et al., 2019).
Reliance on survey data restricts applicability; longitudinal, experimental, and qualitative designs are called for (pp.37-38).

Study 4 raters' affect toward the targets may drive ratings; Trump and Merkel are polarizing figures, and the authors separate positivity from descriptive normativity (p.38, citing Wessels et al., 2020).
Lesser-known politicians are untested (p.38).

Study 2 and Study 3 use general-population samples with neutralized wording ('other people' instead of 'other politicians'; 'work' instead of 'politics') (p.22), so the instrument has not been validated on actual politicians as self-raters.
Study 4 sample is skewed: 76.3% high education, 38.9% female, male-leaning, somewhat left-leaning (p.29).
Dedication & Sacrifice was tested with only two positively worded items and is 'yet to become fully fledged' (p.21).
Several 4-item scales have low reliability (alpha .44-.52 for Loyalty, Humility, Compromise, Creativity in Study 2; Table 2, p.25).
Assertiveness and Loyalty show multidimensionality or reversed items (pp.28-30).
Predictive validity is claimed in the Discussion (p.36) but the evidence is concurrent correlations only.

Inconsistent study labels: Table 2 and Table 3 are labeled Study 1 while the data are from Study 2; Table 4 and Table 5 are labeled Study 3 while the data are from Study 4; the Study 3 section heading is used for the ideal-trait study whereas the discussion labels it Study 3 too. Readers must map labels by content.
Acquiescence control relies on ipsatization and balanced keying; the authors do not report a model-based acquiescence correction.

summary_md:
PoliPers is a working paper (version 0.1, not peer reviewed) that builds a survey inventory of 15 politically relevant personality facets. Examples are Trust & Faith in Others, Compromise & Cooperativeness, Assertiveness & Will to Take Control, Empathy & Compassion, and Integrity & Honesty. Each facet is mapped to the Big Five, HEXACO, VIA, the Agency/Communion "Big Two" and the Aaldering-Vliegenthart leadership traits. The authors test it in four German samples: self-ratings (N=404), ideal-politician ratings (N=589) and crowd ratings of Trump and Merkel (N=211).

Reliability is uneven. Self-rating alphas run from .44 to .87, and Loyalty, Humility and Compromise all fall at or below .51. Assertiveness splits into two factors: the "power-hungry, claims leadership" item loads reversed in ideal ratings, and observer-rating alpha is .40. Observer ratings carry a large evaluative component. Empathy correlates with likeability at r=.70/.76 and Integrity with rated honesty at .70/.80. Rated facets also correlate with the rater's ideological proximity to the target, for example r=.46 between Integrity and proximity for Trump. The paper calls these "predictive validity", but all of them are concurrent associations measured on the same occasion.

The paper matters here because it is the upstream source of the two facet labels in Paul's agency/communion persona codebook (fec/members/agency_communion_llm.py), which feeds the receptivity layer at PERSONA_W 0.30. It does not test how personality affects response to pressure, lobbying, cosponsorship or votes. Its evidence therefore bears on how the persona construct is defined and on rater-bias risks. It gives no support to the susceptibility signs the engine assigns. It also supports two existing design choices: de-identifying text before LLM rating, and modeling halo as a method factor. Transfer is limited by the setting: German raters, two very prominent leaders, and the 2020-21 era.

bearings.paper_claim: PoliPers defines 15 facets. Table 1 maps Assertiveness & Will to take control to AG: Assertiveness and Empathy & Compassion to COM: Warmth, and gives each facet a named opposite pole (Empathy's is Apathy & Indifference).
bearings.paper_location: Table 1, pp.14-16; facet definitions pp.17-21
bearings.system_side: The persona codebook in agency_communion_llm.py uses the PoliPers names for its two cue classes and scores only the positive poles. The codebook names Birkenmaier & Lechner 2025 as its source. PoliPers does not cite that paper (it cites Repke, Birkenmaier & Lechner 2024, a survey-guide reference), so the link runs through shared authorship, not through PoliPers' citations.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The facet definitions transfer as construct definitions. The psychometric evidence does not: it comes from German survey ratings of traits, not from LLM coding of English congressional sentences.
bearings.verifier_note: Facet names, Agency/Communion mapping and opposite poles confirmed in Table 1 and pp.17-21. Corrected provenance: PoliPers does not cite Birkenmaier & Lechner 2025. Code line numbers in the original bearing were off; the codebook starts at line 31 and the positive-pole rule is at line 56.

bearings.paper_claim: The Assertiveness facet is not unidimensional. In ideal-politician ratings (Study 3, N=589) it gave two factors because the 'power-hungry, claims leadership' item loaded reversed, and its alpha was not computed (Table A4). In observer ratings of Trump and Merkel (pooled, Study 4, N=211) its alpha was .40 and omega .48 (Table A7). In ideal ratings Assertiveness was the only facet that differed by politician gender (d=.19, p=.025).
bearings.paper_location: pp.28-30; Table A4 p.70; Table A5 p.74; Table A7 p.79
bearings.system_side: The self-test treats 'I claim leadership and I am not afraid to use power to get results' as a gold agency unit. The sentence-level agency share pools all agency-labelled sentences, including power-claiming ones, into one score.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The split was measured in citizen ratings of traits, not in congressional sentences. Whether power-claiming and leadership-taking cues split in text is untested, so this is a plausibility warning, not a measured defect.
bearings.verifier_note: All numbers confirmed. Table A7 is captioned 'Study 3, real politicians' although it reports Study 4 observer data, and the paper's study labels are inconsistent throughout. The alpha .40 is pooled across the two targets, not a Trump-only or Merkel-only figure.

gaps_exposed: The persona channel collapses PoliPers' 15 facets into 2 cue shares. Facets with the most face relevance to lobbying receptivity have no measure: Compromise & Cooperativeness, Trust & Faith in Others, and Integrity & Honesty. Compromise is approximated only behaviorally, by cooperation_v2.
Opposite poles (indifference, distrust, rigidity) are coded as 'none' rather than as negative evidence, so low communion and missing communion cues are indistinguishable.
There is no check of whether the gold validation panels' ratings track rater partisanship or ideological proximity, which the paper shows contaminates observer trait ratings.

The assumption that the projected persona is what a lobbyist meets is untested. PoliPers measures persona as perceived by voters, and nothing in the system measures how lobbyists or staff perceive members.
The agency construct is not checked for the leadership-claiming versus power-seeking split that PoliPers found in Assertiveness.
flags: Working paper version 0.1, not peer reviewed, with inconsistent study labels and item counts (58 vs 60). Cite with that status.
The paper's 'predictive validity' wording (p.36) describes same-occasion concurrent correlations. Do not quote it as predictive evidence for any member-level forecast.

Nothing in the paper validates the receptivity persona signs (communion means susceptible, agency means resistant). The persona term stays a design prior. PERSONA_W 0.30 is kept by owner ruling, and this paper is not grounds to propose removing it.
No conflict with the SNA rejections (D-021, D-025, D-104..D-108). The paper makes no network, lobbying, or reciprocity claims.
Agent analysis in this note, including the assertiveness-split concern applied to text cues, is UNVERIFIED until reproduced by a second path (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul's note treats Birkenmaier & Lechner as the most direct transfer and names two weaknesses: converting traits into node parameters, and ambiguous statements. PoliPers is the facet framework underneath that codebook, and it sharpens his first worry. It defines facets and shows that their ratings are reliable only in part, but it says nothing about how a facet changes a politician's response to pressure. The trait-to-node conversion (communion susceptible, agency resistant) therefore remains unsupported by this whole literature line. His receptivity note that ten personalities collapse into four observable ones understates the reduction: PoliPers offers 15 facets, and the system uses 2. His notes are not stale, but they do not record that the codebook inherits PoliPers' unstable Assertiveness facet, or that observer-rated persona carries partisan bias.

extraction.title: Legislative Effectiveness in the American States
extraction.venue: American Political Science Review, 119(1), 21-39 (first published online 15 Feb 2024)
extraction.document_type: Empirical journal article (open access, CC BY 4.0): measurement paper with two illustrative studies
extraction.coverage: Read the full extracted text file (all 2,469 lines, front matter through references) in chunks. Metadata hint confirmed: authors, venue, volume and pages, and DOI match the text. The year 2025 is the issue year; online first publication was 15 Feb 2024. Paul's markup: the task listed no markup or annotation files ("(none)"), so paul_markup is empty. The text file carries no highlights or notes. The Supplementary Appendix and PDF were not available, so Tables A1-A12 are referenced in the text but not read.
extraction.research_question: Can individual state legislators' lawmaking effectiveness be measured comparably across 97 state legislative chambers and over time, and does the measure validly capture effectiveness? Two illustrative questions follow: (1) how does the majority-party advantage in lawmaking vary with ideological polarization, majority-party cohesion, and seat-share imbalance? (2) how do institutional designs (pay, professionalism, session length, staff, agenda-control and gatekeeping rules, committee-appointment votes, chamber size, term limits) shape the relative lawmaking power of majority vs minority, chairs vs rank-and-file, and senior vs freshman legislators? (pp. 21-22, 30-34)
extraction.theory: Effectiveness is defined as 'the proven ability to advance a member's agenda items through the legislative process and into law' (Volden and Wiseman 2014, quoted p. 22). It is measured across lawmaking stages, with later and rarer stages weighted more heavily (pp. 22-23). Study 1 draws on conditional party government (Aldrich and Battista 2002): polarization and majority cohesion should raise majority advantage. A competing electoral account says tenuous majorities intensify partisanship (Rosenthal 1998). Median-voter logic predicts moderates do better (Black 1958; Downs 1957; Hitt, Volden and Wiseman 2017). Study 2 is explicitly exploratory with no specific hypotheses; it draws on Anzia and Jackman (2013) for agenda and gatekeeping effects (pp. 30-34).
extraction.data: Sample: 80,344 legislator-term SLES scores across 1,032 chamber-terms (legislative sessions) in 97 state legislative chambers, 1987-2018, built from about 1.8 million bills (p. 21). Kansas is excluded because sponsor names are rarely attached to bills (fn. 1, p. 22). Four states enter after 2003 (MA 2009; NE, OR, RI 2007). Unit for Table 1: legislator-term (72,888 observations with full covariates; 53,846 lower-chamber and 19,042 upper-chamber). Unit for Tables 2 and 3: chamber-term (868 and 874 chamber-terms in Table 2; 776-818 in Table 3). Sources: state government online legislative archives (bill histories and sponsors), LexisNexis and NewsBank newspaper coverage (substantive significance), Shor and McCarty (2011) ideal points (coverage 1993-2016), Anzia and Jackman (2013) procedural rules, and North Carolina NCCPPR rankings for 2005-2012 (Edwards 2018).
extraction.method:
Measure: a weighted average of 15 indicators. These are the shares of a legislator's bills that reach each of five stages (introduced, action in committee, action beyond committee, passed home chamber, became law) at each of three significance levels (commemorative weight 1, substantive weight 5, substantive and significant weight 10). Scores are normalized so each chamber-term has mean 1 (Eq. 1, pp. 23-24). Validity checks: hand-coding audit, North Carolina criterion validation, and construct validation via lagged correlations and OLS. Table 1 is OLS with fixed effects by term and chamber (or state), with standard errors clustered by legislator. Tables 2 and 3 are chamber-level OLS with standard errors clustered by state chamber. Outcomes are the median majority-minus-minority SLES gap, the share of majority members above the minority median, and median differences for chairs vs rank-and-file and non-freshmen vs freshmen. Tests are two-tailed (+p<0.1, *p<0.05, **p<0.01).</method>
<parameter name="identification">No causal identification strategy. Results are associational. Fixed effects absorb state, chamber and term differences. The authors state that endogeneity is unaddressed: rules may be chosen by strong parties, and term limits or professionalism may respond to entrenched power (p. 34). Study 2 is framed as illustrative and exploratory.
extraction.scope: Population: state legislators in 97 chambers (49 states, derived from Kansas exclusion and Nebraska's unicameral chamber), 1987-2018. Institution: state legislatures only. The paper says SLES values should not be compared directly across chambers or eras, because absolute scores are relative to each chamber-term; comparisons of factor effects across settings are appropriate (pp. 23-24). It explicitly does not capture oversight, obstruction, constituency service, or behind-the-scenes lawmaking (fn. 8, p. 24).

Criterion validity: SLES tracks North Carolina's subjective NCCPPR effectiveness rankings and outperforms hit-rate metrics.

limitations: Results are associational. The authors say the institutional-design relationships may face endogeneity (rules chosen by strong parties; term limits or professionalism adopted to weaken entrenched politicians) (p. 34).
Study 2 is explicitly exploratory, with no specific hypotheses tested (p. 34).

Effectiveness excludes oversight, voting for district interests, communication, and obstruction; it also misses behind-the-scenes lawmaking and bills that hitchhike on must-pass legislation (pp. 22, 24, fn. 8).
Absolute SLES values are not comparable across chambers or eras; only relative comparisons of factor effects are recommended (pp. 23-24).

Sponsor attribution for committee bills and multiple-sponsor bills required judgment (fn. 2, p. 22), and some states (Massachusetts by-request bills, Connecticut, Iowa, Idaho committee bills) required case-by-case decisions (p. 23-24).
Substantive significance is coded from newspaper mentions and state-specific dictionaries (p. 23), with a coding error rate of 4.8% before revision (p. 24).
SLES and NCCPPR rankings may tap different concepts; party leaders who act behind the scenes may be underrated by SLES (p. 24).
Caution is urged about women and minority coefficients, which may reflect unmodeled factors (p. 26).
About 8,000 Table 1 observations are lost to missing covariates, and Nebraska's 301 observations are dropped as nonpartisan (fn. 9, p. 25).
Term limits are a binary indicator; binding status and length are not modeled in the main text (fn. 20, p. 34; Table A9 in appendix).
Kansas is excluded for data quality (fn. 1, p. 22).

summary_md:
Bucchianeri, Volden and Wiseman adapt the congressional Legislative Effectiveness Score to state legislatures. The result is the SLES: 80,344 legislator-term scores across 97 chambers, 1987-2018, built from about 1.8 million bills. Each score is a weighted average of 15 indicators: the share of a member's sponsored bills that reach each of five stages (introduced, action in committee, action beyond committee, passed chamber, law), at three significance levels weighted 1, 5 and 10. Scores are normalized to mean 1 within each chamber-term. The authors stress that absolute scores should not be compared across chambers or eras.

They check validity three ways. A hand audit found 95.2% of 49,037 sampled bills correctly coded. In North Carolina (2005-2012), SLES alone explains about half the variance in subjective effectiveness rankings and beats simple hit rates. Scores also persist from term to term (rho 0.38-0.66, highest when majority control does not change). In pooled OLS, majority status adds 0.370 (0.362 lower chamber, 0.387 upper) and a committee chair adds 0.507 (0.609 lower vs 0.307 upper). Moderates are more effective. Two exploratory chamber-level studies find that majority advantage grows with polarization, majority-party cohesion and professionalism. All results are associational.

What this means for Paul's system: the paper is the direct method source for the unactivated effectiveness shadow (fec/engine/legislative_effectiveness.py), which copies the five stages, the 1/5/10 weights and per-chamber-term normalization. The shadow departs from SLES in two ways: it credits cosponsors, and it measures significance by CU mention frequency. The paper's validation evidence therefore does not carry over to those changes. The paper also exposes three weak spots in the live rank:
- Leg% and Influence% are pooled across the House and Senate.
- The efficiency term is the hit-rate kind of measure the paper outperforms.
- Nothing controls for majority status, which the paper finds is the largest structural driver of advancement.

The brain already records that CEL LES is roughly orthogonal to the live score (+0.10 Spearman).

summary_issues: Summary calls both chamber-level studies exploratory. The paper frames only Study 2 as exploratory (lines 1726-1732); Study 1 tests two named hypotheses, conditional party government and insecure majorities (lines 1234-1236, 1434-1435).

Summary says the shadow departs from SLES in two ways. The bearing lists more: cosponsor credit with 180-day timing decay, letters forced to weight 5, a 70/30 composite, and significance from upstream impact data. The claim that significance comes from CU mention frequency was not found in legislative_effectiveness.py.
Gaps section says majority status is the largest structural driver of advancement. Not supported: the pooled chair estimate 0.507 exceeds the majority estimate 0.370 (Table 1 lines 914 and 921).

Ext key finding on Study 1 says a smaller seat-share imbalance widens the majority advantage, which it calls the reverse of the insecure-majority expectation. The paper reads the negative imbalance coefficient (-0.529) as support for insecure majorities (lines 1417-1420, 1459-1461).

Ext key finding says longer sessions are linked to a smaller seniority gap among majority members. Table 3 column 3.3 gives -0.046, not significant; the significant -0.071 is the minority column 3.4 (lines 1893-1896). The same ext also says session length is not significant in the freshman-seniority gap, so ext contradicts itself.

Summary calls the live efficiency term a hit-rate measure that the paper outperforms. The paper's hit-rate comparison is SLES against hit rates in North Carolina; mapping that to the Melange efficiency term is the analyst's inference.

Paul alignment and brain claims are not checked here: paul_entries is empty, the brain was not read under the boot-skip rule, and the claims about Paul's citations, the September shadow commission, the +0.10 CEL LES orthogonality and the not-activated shadow status are unverified and remain open.
Related links: the text does not mention Aref and Neal, Ramey, or Porter, so those three links were dropped. Sotoudeh and Fouirnaies were kept as complements only, not as citations.

Bearing 5 and the gaps section state or imply that minority advancement reflects position rather than effort; the paper measures no effort and is associational (p. 34). The causal reading was removed.

Coverage: the text file was read at the cited lines for all five bearings and all five related links. The Supplementary Appendix and PDF were not available, so Table A4 (NC validation), Table A9 (term limits) and Table A10 were not checked; Figure 6 at p. 30 was not checked.
gaps_exposed: Live Leg% (legacy mode) and Influence% (committee raw/max) pool the House and Senate in one percentile or maximum. summary_md:
Kim's 2018 LobbyView note is a partial technical manual, not an empirical study. It has no estimates, no N and no stated coverage window. It documents how LDA lobbying reports get linked to congressional bills. First, a regex finds bill numbers. Then each mention is assigned to a Congress by taking the argmax of cosine similarity between the candidate bill text and the text around the mention, looking back three Congresses by default; if nothing matches, the code falls back to the filing-year Congress. The Congress is then propagated across the report by majority vote, titles are matched, and close bill numbers (gap of 10 or less) are expanded into ranges. Industries are grouped by NAICS2/SIC for per-industry Herfindahl indices, with Compustat merged in. The note names one failure case: Google's 2013 report cites H.R. 2577, which is a 112th-Congress bill, so the naive filing-year rule gets it wrong. It gives no error rates for any heuristic.

This matters for Paul's lobbying lane in three ways:
1. **Every LobbyView-derived member link is a bill-roster join, not a contact record.** That backs the system's finding that the lobbied-member link is circular.
2. **Paul's own LDA rebuild uses a different bill-resolution rule than the LobbyView pipeline.** A citation without an "of 20XX" suffix binds to the filing-year Congress, which is the naive rule this paper says fails. Hyphenated ranges are not expanded. So the network.csv vintage (2000-2022) and the 2021+ rebuild are different instruments with an unmeasured seam between them.
3. **The paper uses NAICS as an industry grouping.** The system has ruled NAICS to be linkage metadata only.

None of this is a validation of anything. The heuristics' accuracy is unreported, and the argmax always returns an answer.

extraction.research_question: Can network centrality computed from co-voting records (correlations between members' voting records) identify the actual cue-provider or leader in a legislature, and in particular does a proposed absolute-value centrality measure separate cue-providers from followers and majoritarians where the traditional centrality approach cannot? (Inferred from the appendix; the main question is stated in the published article, which is not in this text.)
extraction.theory: Leader or cue-provider theory: a leader whose followers vote with her some percentage of the time (ally followers, opponent followers, or others at other rates). The appendix argues the leader should have the highest network centrality in a co-voting network built from phi correlations of voting records (lines 318-353). Majoritarians are members who vote with the majority; the traditional centrality approach can rank majoritarians above the actual cue-provider (Figure 4 text, line 303).
extraction.data: Empirical data (Table 1, line 12-120): 940 MEP observations (centrality N = 897 after network construction; left-right distance to EP median N = 868; pro/anti-EU distance to EP median N = 872). Unit is the MEP. Variables include centrality (mean .283, SD .138, range .006-.502), party leader (mean .05), committee leader (.09), EP leader (.03), coordinator (.23), reports drafted (mean 1.05), reports amended (6.73), opinions (.72), motions (6.82), speeches (29.07), questions (20.07), declarations (.58), tenure (1.58), party size (172.01), female (.30). Period of the European Parliament data is not stated in the appendix text. Simulated data (Figures 1-6, lines 289-313): 1000 simulated networks per network class (simple, moderate, complex); 1000 simulations; 100 legislators; 1000 rounds of voting in the Figure 5 runs. Figure 6 uses three parameterizations: US (1 cue-provider, 1 majoritarian, 40 allies, 40 opponents, 20 others at 50%), Supermajority (1 cue-provider, 1 majoritarian, 67 allies, 33 opponents), and EP (1 cue-provider, 1 majoritarian, 37 allies, 25 opponents, 38 others at varied rates, roughly the seven-party EP seat allotment).
extraction.method: Centrality is built from pairwise phi correlations of binary voting records (Table 1 is the 2x2 contingency table underlying phi, lines 331-341). The appendix uses an absolute-value version of this centrality, referred to as the "posterior" measure, which is compared with the traditional (signed) centrality calculation. Analytic method: Hypothesis 1 (leader centrality >= follower centrality) is proved algebraically for a three-voter legislature (leader plus two followers) with follow probabilities q2 and q3 and leader Yes-probability p; the condition reduces to q2 < 1 and q3 < 1 (lines 319-345). The result is extended to n voters by a term-by-term comparison, arguing that each phi term depends only on p and the relevant follow probabilities, so it is unchanged as voters are added (lines 347-353). Simulation method: Monte Carlo generation of cueing networks in three complexity classes, computing the posterior centrality from simulated voting records and correlating it with betweenness, closeness, and weighted degree (Figure 5); and t-tests of cue-provider centrality against the maximum follower and a majoritarian across rounds of voting (Figure 6). Figures 1-4 show cue-provider centrality as a function of follow probabilities.
extraction.scope: Population: members of the European Parliament (party groups named in Table 2: EPP, EPP-ED, PES, ALDE, G/EFA, EUL/NGL, IND/DEM, UEN), plus stylized simulated legislatures (US, supermajority, and EP-style). Institution: European Parliament (empirical) and abstract legislatures (theory). Era: not stated in the appendix text. The theoretical result is stated for single-party legislatures under the stated assumptions.

summary_md:
This is the online appendix to Ringe and Wilson's paper on co-voting centrality. It holds a proof, simulations and descriptive tables from the European Parliament. The authors build a network from pairwise phi correlations of members' binary voting records. They score each member by an absolute-value (sign-blind) centrality: a member followed reliably by allies (positive phi) or reliably opposed by opponents (negative phi) both count toward that member's centrality.

**Proof.** For a single-party legislature, they show the leader's centrality is at least as high as any follower's. The condition reduces to q2 < 1 and q3 < 1. The inequalities are weak (greater than or equal), although the n-voter text says "greater".

**Simulations.** There were 1,000 networks per complexity class, with 100 legislators and 1,000 voting rounds.
- The absolute-value measure separates the cue-provider from followers and from "majoritarians" (members who usually vote with the majority).
- The traditional signed measure can rank majoritarians above the true cue-provider when a third group follows at 35% (Figure 4).
- The measure correlates highly with closeness and weighted degree (no coefficient reported), but only about 0.25 with betweenness.
- Moderate and complex networks lose structure when converted to voting data.
- The authors say the results are "highly dependent on parameterization".

**Empirical side.** The data cover 897 MEPs with centrality scores (mean .283). The parliamentary term is not stated in the appendix.

**Why it matters here.**
- Melange has one co-voting layer: the signed vote backbone in the Draft Systems R script, plus its party-controlled Option C. That layer found the raw signed backbone was about 95% party, then dropped the negative side. The paper offers a mechanism for the first finding (the signed measure rewards majoritarians) and an argument against the second (negative ties carry cue-provider information).
- The paper also clarifies the June 2026 retirement of cosponsor centrality from the Influence pillar. The paper treats sign-blindness as a property of a leadership measure, not as a flaw. That supports the system's two-axis rule, which keeps influence and alignment as separate axes.
- None of this transfers directly. The evidence is analytic and simulated, with European Parliament data, and it concerns co-voting, not cosponsorship.

The absolute-value measure corrects this. In simulation, cue-provider centrality is lowest when both follow probabilities are 50 percent and highest as they approach 0 or 1.

flags: The paper's title frames co-voting centrality as 'a measure of political influence'. If adopted, any centrality rank must be worded as a heuristic model output, never as closeness, access or an influence probability (D-025).

The paper does not argue for either REJECTED SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges, or per-edge volume normalization). Phi correlation is a per-pair standardized agreement on votes, not a reweighting of cosponsor edges, so it must not be cited as support for per-edge volume normalization.

The component description for melange-sna.signed-coalitions says 'signed backbone' (vote-based), but fec/network/signed_coalitions.py:6-8 partitions the signed mention layer (member_references.json). The empirical evidence comes from European Parliament MEPs (term not stated) and the rest is simulation. Any claim transferred to the US House or Senate is UNVERIFIED (DE-062). The proof gives weak inequalities only and is restricted to a single-party legislature.
The empirical leader ranking pools 897 MEPs across party groups. Table 2 gives within-group leaders, but the overall rank is UNSTRATIFIED across the party fault line (the top 17 are all EPP).
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotation on this paper. His centrality-component position is that more research on forms of centrality is needed (Ardekani), that directionality matters (Haythornthwaite), and that eigenvector centrality is not a strong indicator of bill passage (Sotoudeh highlight). The paper partly cuts against reading 'direction-blind' as a defect: it argues that sign-blindness is what lets centrality find cue-providers, which fits the system's own influence-versus-alignment two-axis rule. It agrees with Paul's call for more centrality forms, offering co-voting absolute-value centrality as a candidate he has not considered. His notes are not stale. However, the system's June decision to keep only positive cross-party vote-backbone edges is a choice his notes never address, and this paper bears on it directly.

summary_md:
An unsigned internal memo dated 12/10/2025. Names are redacted and it is not peer-reviewed. It profiles federal political giving by the top 10 firms by revenue in four industries: life insurance, mutual funds, credit unions and commercial banking. It splits that giving across CEOs, other executives, company PACs, trade associations (ACLI, ACU, ABA) and the four largest Super PACs. Its headline claim is that firms push political spending onto executives and adjust their giving to executive-branch scrutiny "regardless of party". The evidence is per-industry dollar averages, which carry no cycle years, source or N, plus news-driven case stories: Bank of America after the DOJ probe, JPMorgan's PAC memos, and the Schwab charity fund. There is no comparison group and no test. The memo reports its own ranking contradictions, and it uses "dark money" to mean Super PAC money.

For Paul's systems the memo is a descriptive input, not evidence. Its unit of analysis is the same one Mentat's spending-statistics sheet already builds. That sheet has role tiers (Chief, Middle Management, Employee, Corporate) and channel columns (Super PAC, Company PAC, Trade Association, Candidate, Company PAC to Super PAC, each with a partisan split). Mentat also ingests a "Credit Union Cross Industry Spending.xlsx" template. The memo may therefore come from the same product line, and if it does it is not an independent check. Two parts are useful. First, the bank, mutual-fund and CU stories show giving moving into channels that per-member models never see: trade associations, Super PACs, and family or charity vehicles. That bears on how Melange's flip model measures competitor money. Second, its partisan readings of Super PAC money ignore whether the money supported or opposed a candidate, which Mentat already separates. Every figure in the memo should be treated as UNVERIFIED, with no window or denominator.

The flag that the memo may come from the Mentat product line rests only on a layout resemblance; the item holds no evidence of lineage and it should stay an open question.

gaps_exposed: Melange's flip and break-even money legs see only direct PAC-to-member dollars (cu, banks + finserv). Trade-association and Super PAC independent-expenditure money targeted at a member is absent, and the memo argues those are the main bank and mutual-fund channels.

Mentat has no linkage from roster executives to their personal or charitable vehicles (foundations, donor-advised funds, family entities). Giving that an executive redirects off the employer field goes unattributed.
No study variable captures executive-branch enforcement or scrutiny events (DOJ probes, executive orders). The sector-growth SHIFT tests cover congressional control only.

No figure for within-industry volatility of giving by channel. The memo calls mutual funds the most volatile, which bears on forecast interval width, but the forecast reports no per-industry dispersion.
flags: UNVERIFIED (DE-062): every dollar figure in the memo lacks a source, cycle window, N and denominator, which breaks the rule that every figure names its window and denominator. Quote none of them without that label.

The memo may not be independent of the system. Its channel and role layout matches Mentat's spending-statistics sheet (report.R:64-80), and Mentat ingests a 'Credit Union Cross Industry Spending.xlsx' template (ingest.R:1294). If it was built from Mentat output, it cannot serve as a second path that reproduces Mentat.
Terminology conflict: the memo calls Super PAC donations 'dark money'. Mentat keeps Super PAC money (FEC-disclosed) separate from 501(c) and 527 money. Do not import the memo's wording.

The memo's partisan readings of Super PAC money ignore support/oppose direction, and the brain records that 89% of beneficiary dollars were oppose-coded. 'GOP-aligned' destinations do not equal pro-GOP spending.

The causal claim (executive-branch pressure drives giving 'regardless of party') rests on narrative and timing. It sits uneasily with the memo's own GOP-tilted mutual-fund finding, and its ranking contradictions are unreconciled (bank CEO $16,781 called 1st, below the mutual-fund CEO's $17,882).
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this memo. It loosely agrees with his reading of strategic, cycle-aware giving (Bacik: more money in election years; Furnas: party-tied firms lose when that party loses). It also agrees with his wish to map rival industries (banks and funds against CUs). But it supplies only industry averages and anecdotes, with no member-level allocation. It cannot answer his 'conflicting industries' note for the industry boards or the flip model. The system's own SHIFT result found no stable partisan shift with expected control. That cuts against generalizing the memo's 'adapt to whoever holds power' story, though the memo concerns the executive branch, which SHIFT does not test. If Paul or his team wrote this memo, its framing of channel substitution is now better covered by Mentat's role and channel columns and the support/oppose partition than the memo's own figures. The memo should be read as a framing document, not as evidence.

related.why: Paul-authored cross-industry finance and lobbying report (author Goff) covering credit unions and community banks. Overlap with this memo may be real, but the memo names are redacted, so shared data lineage is unverified.

Furnas, LaPira and Brock find low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC spending. That supports the memo's premise that money moves across channels and warns against treating one channel as total effort.
Irvin (2023) studies dark-money vehicles among 501(c)(4) advocacy groups, using dark money for nonprofit non-disclosure. The memo instead uses the term for disclosed Super PAC donations.

Couch, Fox and Everton (2016) model a single dark-money network and rank nodes with AHP/TOPSIS. It is a network view of dark money, not a model of the memo's reservoir claim, so the link to Mentat's transfer graph is loose.

Kim, Stuckatz and Wolters (2020) link donations to lobbying for interest group-politician pairs and report firm-level executive and employee giving in Appendix C. That is a more rigorous version of the executive-giving question, not the same design.
